cotton_bacterial_blight.name: Cotton Bacterial Blight
cotton_bacterial_blight.description: A bacterial disease that can affect leaves, stems and sometimes bolls of cotton.
symptoms: Small water-soaked or angular lesions on leaves
Lesions may become dark brown or black
Leaf spots may enlarge and cause premature leaf damage
Stem or boll lesions may occur in severe infections
causes: Bacterial infection
Infected seed or plant debris can contribute to disease spread
Warm, humid and wet conditions favor bacterial disease development
favorable_conditions: Frequent rainfall or prolonged leaf wetness
prevention: Use resistant or tolerant varieties where available
management: Remove and destroy severely infected plant material
Avoid unnecessary overhead irrigation
Use locally recommended bactericidal or copper-based products only according to the current agricultural label
Consult a local agricultural extension officer for chemical recommendations
cotton_bacterial_blight.source_status: Verify current local recommendation before chemical treatment

cotton_curl_virus.name: Cotton Leaf Curl Virus
cotton_curl_virus.description: A viral disease of cotton associated with leaf-curling symptoms and transmitted primarily by whiteflies.
symptoms: Upward or downward curling of leaves
Leaf thickening and distortion
Enlarged veins or vein swelling
Reduced plant growth in severe infections
causes: Cotton leaf curl virus infection
Spread is associated with whitefly vectors
prevention: Grow recommended tolerant or resistant varieties
Remove severely infected plants when recommended locally
Control whitefly populations using integrated pest management
management: There is no direct cure that eliminates the virus from an infected plant
Focus on controlling the vector and removing sources of infection
Follow locally recommended whitefly management practices
cotton_curl_virus.source_status: Verify current regional cotton leaf curl recommendations

cotton_fussarium_wilt.name: Cotton Fusarium Wilt
cotton_fussarium_wilt.description: A soil-associated wilt disease that interferes with water movement and can cause progressive yellowing and wilting.
symptoms: Yellowing of leaves
Wilting of leaves and shoots
Stunted plant growth
Vascular discoloration may be visible when stems are cut
Severely affected plants may die
causes: Fusarium species in soil or infected planting material
The pathogen can persist in soil and crop residues
favorable_conditions: Plant stress and poor crop management
prevention: Use resistant or tolerant varieties where available
management: Remove severely affected plants and residues where practical
Use resistant varieties
Maintain balanced crop nutrition
Follow locally recommended biological or chemical management practices

cotton_healthy.name: Healthy Cotton Plant
cotton_healthy.description: The plant shows no characteristic visual symptoms of the diseases represented in the classifier.
management: No disease treatment is indicated based on this classification
Continue routine crop monitoring

groundnut_early_leaf_spot.name: Groundnut Early Leaf Spot
groundnut_early_leaf_spot.description: A foliar fungal disease of groundnut characterized by brown leaf lesions, often with a chlorotic halo.
symptoms: Sub-circular to irregular dark-brown lesions
Brown spots commonly occur on the upper leaflet surface
A yellow or chlorotic halo may surround lesions
Severe infection causes leaf yellowing, necrosis and premature defoliation
causes: Cercospora arachidicola
The pathogen can survive in infected plant debris
management: Use locally recommended fungicides when disease pressure warrants treatment
Rotate fungicide modes of action to reduce resistance risk
Follow current agricultural label instructions

groundnut_early_rust.name: Groundnut Rust
groundnut_early_rust.description: A rust disease of groundnut that produces reddish-brown to orange pustules, especially on leaf surfaces.
symptoms: Orange or reddish-brown pustules
Pustules commonly develop on the lower leaf surface
Leaves become necrotic and dry
Severe infection can reduce the functional leaf area
causes: Puccinia arachidis
favorable_conditions: Extended periods favorable for fungal infection
management: Use locally recommended fungicides when required
Monitor fields regularly for rust pustules
Follow current agricultural label instructions

groundnut_healthy_leaf.name: Healthy Groundnut Plant
groundnut_healthy_leaf.description: The plant does not show characteristic symptoms of the groundnut diseases represented in the classifier.
management: No disease treatment is indicated based on this classification
Continue routine crop monitoring

groundnut_late_leaf_spot.name: Groundnut Late Leaf Spot
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.description: A major foliar disease of groundnut characterized by dark lesions, particularly on the lower leaf surface.
symptoms: Dark circular to nearly circular lesions
Black or dark lesions are commonly visible on the lower leaf surface
Lesions may lack the prominent yellow halo associated with early leaf spot
Severe infection causes yellowing, necrosis and premature defoliation
causes: Phaeoisariopsis personata, also known as Neopseudocercospora personata in modern taxonomy
management: Use locally recommended fungicide programs when required
Rotate fungicide modes of action
Monitor regularly because late leaf spot may occur together with rust
groundnut_late_leaf_spot.source_status: ICAR-CCARI and ICAR groundnut disease resources

groundnut_late_rust.name: Groundnut Rust
groundnut_late_rust.description: Groundnut rust produces characteristic orange to reddish-brown pustules and can cause severe leaf damage.
symptoms: Orange or reddish-brown pustules on leaves
Pustules are often prominent on lower leaf surfaces
Leaves become necrotic and dry
Severe disease reduces photosynthetic leaf area
causes: Puccinia arachidis
management: Use locally recommended fungicide treatments when necessary
Follow current label instructions
Avoid repeated use of the same fungicide mode of action

groundnut_nutrition_deficiency.name: Groundnut Nutrient Deficiency
groundnut_nutrition_deficiency.description: A visual category representing nutrient-related symptoms rather than a single infectious disease.
symptoms: Leaf yellowing or chlorosis
Abnormal leaf coloration
Reduced growth or vigor
Symptoms vary substantially depending on the nutrient involved
causes: Insufficient availability of one or more essential nutrients
Soil pH or salinity can affect nutrient availability
Unbalanced fertilization
favorable_conditions: Soil conditions that limit nutrient uptake
prevention: Apply balanced fertilizers based on crop and soil requirements
Maintain suitable soil pH and moisture
management: Identify the specific nutrient deficiency before treatment
Use soil or plant analysis where possible
Apply the deficient nutrient at locally recommended rates
groundnut_nutrition_deficiency.source_status: Requires field/soil confirmation; not a single disease diagnosis

ragi_downy.name: Ragi Downy Mildew
ragi_downy.description: A downy mildew disease that can affect finger millet, particularly under favorable humid conditions.
symptoms: Pale or chlorotic areas on leaves
Downy growth may develop under humid conditions
Plants may become weak or stunted
Severe infection can reduce grain formation
causes: Downy mildew pathogen
Disease development is favored by humid conditions
management: Remove severely affected plants when practical
Use locally recommended disease-management products if necessary
Follow current agricultural recommendations
ragi_downy.source_status: ICAR and TNAU finger millet disease resources

ragi_healthy.name: Healthy Ragi Plant
ragi_healthy.description: The plant does not show characteristic symptoms of the ragi diseases represented in the classifier.
management: No disease treatment is indicated based on this classification

ragi_mottle.name: Ragi Mottle Streak
ragi_mottle.description: A viral disease category associated with chlorotic streaking, mottling and reduced plant vigor.
symptoms: Chlorotic streaks or mottled patterns on leaves
Pale or weakened plants
Stunted growth
Poorly developed or poorly filled earheads in severe cases
causes: Finger millet virus or mottle-streak virus complex
Vector transmission can contribute to spread
prevention: Remove heavily infected plants where recommended
Manage insect vectors using integrated pest management
management: There is no direct cure for an infected plant
Focus on vector management and removal of infection sources

ragi_seedling.name: Ragi Seedling Blight
ragi_seedling.description: A disease affecting ragi seedlings and young plants, with brown lesions that may enlarge and merge.
symptoms: Small oval or elongated brown leaf spots
Spots can enlarge and merge into larger lesions
Dark brown lesions may cause leaf blighting
The disease can affect leaves, culms, leaf sheaths, neck and panicles
causes: Helminthosporium nodulosum is reported as a causal organism for seedling blight/leaf spot
prevention: Use appropriate seed treatment where recommended
management: Remove severely affected seedlings where practical
Use locally recommended fungicide or biological treatments
Follow current agricultural label recommendations

ragi_smut.name: Ragi Smut
ragi_smut.description: A smut disease affecting the grain-bearing portions of finger millet.
symptoms: Dark or black smut masses replacing or affecting grains
Affected fingers or grain-bearing structures may become discolored
Grain quality and yield can be reduced
causes: Smut fungus infecting the reproductive structures
favorable_conditions: Presence of infected seed or inoculum
Favorable moisture conditions during susceptible growth stages
prevention: Use recommended resistant varieties where available
management: Use appropriate seed treatment
Remove and destroy heavily infected earheads
Follow locally recommended fungicide or biological management

ragi_wilt.name: Ragi Wilt or Foot Rot
ragi_wilt.description: A wilt or foot-rot disease that can cause weakening, yellowing and death of ragi plants.
symptoms: Yellowing and wilting
Weakening near the base of the plant
Root or basal tissue damage
Plants may die in patches under severe disease
causes: Soil-associated fungal pathogens
Disease can be favored by stressed plants and poor soil conditions
management: Improve soil and water management
Use biological or chemical treatments recommended locally
Use tolerant varieties where available

rice_sheath_blight.name: Rice Sheath Blight
rice_sheath_blight.description: A fungal disease caused by Rhizoctonia solani that primarily affects leaf sheaths and can spread upward through the canopy.
symptoms: Oval or ellipsoidal greenish-gray lesions on leaf sheaths
Lesions later develop gray-white centers and brown margins
Lesions can spread upward to leaves
Severely affected leaves dry and die
causes: Rhizoctonia solani
management: Reduce excessive canopy density
Manage water appropriately
Use locally recommended fungicides when required

rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.name: Rice Bacterial Leaf Blight
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.description: A bacterial disease that causes water-soaked lesions and progressive drying of rice leaves.
symptoms: Water-soaked lesions near leaf margins or tips
Lesions expand and become yellow to straw colored
Leaves may dry from the tip downward
Severe infection can cause wilting and plant death, particularly in young plants
causes: Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae
prevention: Use healthy seed and planting material
management: Remove or manage sources of infection
Avoid practices that injure plants
Use locally recommended bactericide or integrated disease-management measures

rice_brown_spot.name: Rice Brown Spot
rice_brown_spot.description: A fungal leaf and grain disease characterized by brown lesions and commonly associated with stressed or nutritionally deficient plants.
symptoms: Small circular to oval brown lesions on leaves
Lesions may have darker margins
Severe infection causes leaf necrosis
The disease can also affect grains
causes: Bipolaris oryzae
management: Correct nutrient deficiencies
Improve water management
Use locally recommended fungicides when disease pressure warrants treatment

rice_healthy.name: Healthy Rice Plant
rice_healthy.description: The plant does not show characteristic symptoms of the rice diseases represented in the classifier.
management: No disease treatment is indicated based on this classification

rice_leaf_blast.name: Rice Blast
rice_leaf_blast.description: A major fungal disease that can affect leaves, collars, nodes and necks of rice plants.
symptoms: Spindle or diamond-shaped lesions on leaves
Lesions often have gray or whitish centers and darker margins
Neck infection can cause panicles to fall over
Severe infection can produce whiteheads and poor grain formation
causes: Magnaporthe oryzae
favorable_conditions: Excessive nitrogen can increase disease intensity
prevention: Use appropriate planting time and crop management
management: Use resistant varieties where available
Manage nitrogen carefully
Use locally recommended fungicides when required
Pay particular attention to disease at heading and neck stages

rice_leaf_scald.name: Rice Leaf Scald
rice_leaf_scald.description: A foliar disease that produces scald-like lesions and can reduce functional leaf area.
symptoms: Large brown or grayish lesions on leaves
Lesions may begin at leaf tips or margins
Older lesions may become pale or straw colored
Severe infection can cause extensive leaf drying
causes: Fungal pathogen associated with rice leaf scald
management: Remove infected residues where practical
Improve crop ventilation
Use locally recommended fungicides only when necessary
rice_leaf_scald.source_status: IRRI rice disease resources; verify local recommendation

sugarcane_healthy.name: Healthy Sugarcane Plant
sugarcane_healthy.description: The plant does not show characteristic symptoms of the sugarcane diseases represented in the classifier.
prevention: Maintain balanced nutrition and water management
management: No disease treatment is indicated based on this classification
Continue routine field monitoring

sugarcane_mosaic.name: Sugarcane Mosaic
sugarcane_mosaic.description: A viral disease characterized mainly by mosaic or mottled patterns on sugarcane leaves.
symptoms: Light and dark green mosaic patterns on leaves
Leaf mottling or streaking
Reduced vigor in susceptible varieties
Severe infection can reduce cane yield
causes: Sugarcane mosaic virus and related mosaic viruses
Infected planting material is an important source
prevention: Remove severely infected clumps when recommended
management: There is no direct cure for an infected plant
Use clean planting material and resistant varieties
Manage vectors where appropriate

sugarcane_redrot.name: Sugarcane Red Rot
sugarcane_redrot.description: A serious fungal disease of sugarcane that causes characteristic reddish discoloration inside infected stalks.
symptoms: Leaves change from green to orange or yellow and dry from the bottom upward
Affected canes may show external discoloration
Splitting an infected stalk reveals reddish internal tissue with intermittent white patches
Pith may become discolored and may develop an unpleasant odor
causes: Colletotrichum falcatum, historically also referred to as Glomerella tucumanensis
prevention: Use resistant or moderately resistant varieties
management: Do not use infected canes as planting material
Remove and destroy affected clumps
Use recommended sett treatment
Follow local sugarcane disease-management recommendations

sugarcane_rust.name: Sugarcane Rust
sugarcane_rust.description: A foliar fungal disease producing yellow, brown or reddish-brown rust-like lesions and pustules.
symptoms: Small elongated yellowish spots
Spots become brown, orange-brown or red-brown
Rust-colored pustules may develop on leaves
Severe infection can cause premature leaf death
causes: Puccinia erianthi
management: Monitor for rust pustules
Use locally recommended fungicides when disease pressure warrants treatment
Follow current agricultural label instructions

sugarcane_yellow.name: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Disease
sugarcane_yellow.description: A viral disease characterized by yellowing of leaf midribs and adjacent leaf tissue, followed by drying and reduced cane growth.
symptoms: Yellowing of the midrib and adjacent leaf tissue
Yellowing and drying of leaves around the upper canopy
Severe cases may show spindle drying and bunching at the top
Stunted cane growth and reduced internode elongation
causes: Sugarcane yellow leaf virus
The virus can be transmitted by aphid vectors and infected planting material
prevention: Use resistant or tolerant varieties where available
Use healthy nursery or tissue-culture planting material
management: There is no direct cure for an infected plant
Use healthy planting material
Manage aphid vectors using integrated pest management
Remove severely affected material where locally recommended
sugarcane_yellow.source_status: TNAU and ICAR sugarcane disease resources
